summary: In 1969, Apollo 11 left a mirror on the Moon, and observatories still bounce lasers off it today. The Mirror That Still Answers is a six-and-a-half-minute cartoon, drawn like a 1930s short, in which that mirror tells children aged 8 to 12 about the machines NASA left behind. For the Abandoned but not Forgotten challenge, it introduces two neighbors that stopped answering: the Opportunity rover on Mars and the Pioneer 10 probe. Every scene runs on NASA data. The viewer's light takes as long to return as a real 2026 laser measurement from the NASA CDDIS archive. Opportunity's sky darkens with the rover's own dust readings from the Planetary Data System. Pioneer 10's distance is calculated from JPL Horizons for the day the film is watched. It matters because children hear claims all day: the film answers a question a child in one of our families asked, how do we know what we know?, with measurements anyone can check.
details:
The film. A cartoon of about six and a half minutes that runs in the browser, narrated in English by a team member. The viewer takes part three times: sending light to the Moon, sliding through Opportunity's days on Mars, and sending a greeting to Pioneer 10. It opens on a real Apollo 11 photograph of Tranquility Base, which turns into a cartoon Moon where the reflector is asleep.

Chapter 1, the Mirror. The viewer's pulse of light takes 2.505444 seconds to come back: the round trip of the most recent laser measurement in NASA's archive as of November 14, 2026, made from Grasse, France, on July 7, 2026. One cartoon photon returns for each of the 56 photons that station counted over about ten minutes of laser shots. The Mirror then explains that half of that time, multiplied by the speed of light, is the distance to the Moon, and shows all 275 measurements from 2025 and 2026 on a cinema screen, plotted over the Moon's orbit from JPL Horizons.

Chapter 2, Opportunity. The colour of the Martian sky, the brightness of the Sun and the amount of dust in the air come from the rover's atmospheric opacity, measured on 4,674 days, in the NASA Planetary Data System. The viewer can slide through those days. The 2007 dust storm, and the planet-wide storm of 2018 after which the rover fell silent, are played from the same numbers.

Chapter 3, Pioneer 10. Using JPL Horizons, the film works out how far the probe is on the day it is watched (about 141 times the Earth-Sun distance) and how long a greeting would take to reach it (about 19 hours 36 minutes). Its path since 1972 is drawn month by month from the same data.

Why we made it. Children hear claims all day, and the question that started this project came from one of them. The film's answer is a measurement anyone can repeat or look up, and the machines we left behind are the ones still providing it. It ends on that idea: some of them still answer, some went quiet, and every one left something you can check.

How we made it. HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no framework, hosted on GitHub Pages. A small canvas engine handles the camera, the frame-by-frame drawings, particles and the old-film look. The animation follows Disney's twelve principles and is timed to each recorded word. Python scripts turn the NASA files into the tables the film reads. Code and data (MIT license): https://github.com/danelerr/the-mirror-that-still-answers

Accessibility. Captions on by default, a "Check the data" panel with links to every NASA source and the sums to redo, an option to turn off the film flicker (off by default when the system asks for reduced motion), buttons and a slider that work with the keyboard, and a chapter bar to jump to any part.

Use of AI. The team chose the challenge, the audience, the question and the 1930s style, and picked the characters from options an AI assistant suggested (the Apollo 11 reflector as narrator was one of them). AI image generators made the character drawings, the frame-by-frame sheets and the painted backgrounds from our prompts. ACE-Step 1.5 made the two music pieces. An AI assistant drafted the script, which we edited and checked against NASA sources, and an AI coding assistant wrote the code under our direction. The voice, the NASA photographs and the NASA data are not AI-generated, and the film shows an AI notice on screen at all times.
dataRefs: Lunar laser ranging to the Apollo 11 retroreflector, 2025-2026 (NASA CDDIS, ILRS archive, npt_crd_v2/apollo11)
Apollo 11 Laser Ranging Retroreflector, NSSDCA experiment 1969-059C-04
NASA/JPL Horizons: Earth-Moon distance (target 301) and Pioneer 10 distance and light time (target -23)
Opportunity Pancam atmospheric opacity, 2004-2018 (NASA PDS Geosciences Node)
PIA22930: Opportunity's last reading, tau about 10.8 (NASA/JPL-Caltech)
NASA photos: AS11-40-5948, AS17-148-22727, art002e009057, PIA17759, ARC-1972-AC72-2135, ARC-1972-AC72-1354 (NASA Image and Video Library)
projectRefs: ILRS laser stations that made the measurements: Observatoire de la Cote d'Azur, Grasse (France) and Apache Point Observatory (USA)
Source code and data tables of this project (MIT license)
Google Gemini image generation (Nano Banana), used in the Gemini app and Google Antigravity: frame-by-frame sprite sheets
Z-Image-Turbo (AI image model, Apache 2.0, run locally): painted scenes
ACE-Step 1.5 (AI music model, MIT license, run locally): the two music pieces
NVIDIA Parakeet TDT 0.6b v3 (speech recognition): timing the animation to each spoken word
FFmpeg: audio cleanup and video assembly
Playwright: automated tests and frame-by-frame video recording
Real-ESRGAN (AI upscaler, BSD 3-Clause, run locally): enlarged some sprite sheets
Pillow, NumPy and SciPy: image processing and data conversion scripts
OpenAI Whisper (speech recognition, MIT license): cross-checking the voice takes
